article.overview: An in-situ material testing system is a payload concept for measuring how lunar regolith behaves where it lies, rather than in a sample that is later analysed on Earth. Its measurements typically cover bearing strength, shear resistance, density and resistance to digging. Historical examples include the Apollo penetrometer work and the Surveyor soil mechanics sampler. The sources reviewed for this article also describe a laboratory device proposed for rover use and a NASA patent-pending robotic multi-tool. No single design is standard, and the sources do not give a verified mass, power or lander compatibility for any example.
article.description: Lunar surface material is loose, layered and variable. The Apollo 14 soil-mechanics study reported that shallow soil characteristics varied more than expected, both laterally and with depth [2]. Engineering properties of this material influence landing pads, roads, foundations, excavation and any in-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) process that digs, sieves or compacts it. Measurements made in place avoid some of the disturbance that comes with collecting and transporting a sample, which is the motivation for in-situ testing. The name in-situ material testing system is the catalogue working name. The sources reviewed use terms such as soil mechanics experiment, self-recording penetrometer, in-situ direct shear device and regolith utilization multi-tool.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to measure properties that control how regolith supports loads and resists movement: bearing strength, shear strength (cohesion and internal friction angle), density, angle of repose and resistance to excavation. Apollo-era penetrometer analysis used bearing-capacity theory, with factors adjusted for cone shape, to estimate strength parameters, and concluded that porosity appeared to be the dominant variable controlling strength for a given soil [6]. Surveyor-era sampler tests recorded motor current during bearing and trenching, which was converted to forces using preflight calibrations [1]. A shear device of the kind described by Jerves and colleagues produces Coulomb parameters (cohesion and internal friction angle) and Bekker parameters for vehicle-terrain analysis [4]. For ISRU and construction, the NASA multi-tool pairs excavation, sieving and compaction with shear, pressure-sinkage, angle-of-repose and density measurements [5]. Applications therefore include site characterisation for landing and mobility, checks on feedstock for regolith processing, and validation of laboratory simulant behaviour against flight data [3].
article.operating_principle: Three measurement approaches recur. Penetration tests push a cone or plate into the soil while force and depth are recorded. The Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer was analysed with bearing-capacity theory [6]. Shear tests move a box or blade relative to the soil to measure resistance to sliding. The Caltech device uses an open-bottomed inner box inside an open-bottomed outer box. Both are lowered into the material, and two rotating plates on the outer box swing outward so the inner box can shear without resistance from the surrounding soil [4]. Excavation tests measure the force needed to dig, scrape or trench. The Surveyor sampler inferred these forces from motor current [1]. A laboratory replica of the Surveyor sampler used a six-axis load cell to record three-dimensional forces and torques, video to follow flow and surcharge formation, and surface profiling to measure deformation [3]. The electronics, data handling and control architecture of a flight system are not described in the sources reviewed.
article.scientific_importance: Regolith properties affect landing hazards, rover traction, excavation energy and the performance of ISRU processes. The Apollo 14 studies reported a density range of 1.45 to 1.60 g/cm3 for the Fra Mauro region, and lower-bound cohesion estimates of 0.03 to 0.10 kN/m2, which the authors compared with 0.35 to 0.70 kN/m2 at previous missions [2]. These figures show that strength varies between sites and with depth, so single-site or laboratory-only data are not enough. Surveyor 7 sampler results indicated that the soil near Tycho behaved quantitatively like the Surveyor 3 site but appeared more deformable and less brittle [1]. Repeated, well-documented in-situ measurements help separate real site-to-site differences from instrument or method effects.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an in-situ material testing system. The examples below cover flown hardware, a historical measurement programme, a laboratory prototype and a proposed robotic tool. The reviewed sources did not publish mass, power or dimensions for most of them, so those fields are recorded as not publicly specified rather than estimated.

examples.name: Surveyor soil mechanics surface sampler
examples.description: The Surveyor soil mechanics surface sampler was an extendable scoop with a bearing-plate attachment that flew on 1960s Surveyor missions [3]. Scott and Roberson describe the Surveyor 7 sampler as essentially identical to the Surveyor 3 sampler, built by the Hughes Aircraft Company, and state that it performed flawlessly on the Moon across an operating temperature range of +180 °F to −167 °F (approximately +82 °C to −111 °C) [1]. Bearing and trenching tests recorded motor current, and forces were calculated from it using preflight calibrations. The abstract does not give the force values [1]. Mass, dimensions and scoop size are not given in the source [1]. The same sampler also freed a jammed alpha-scattering sensor head, which was then moved to analyse a rock and later subsurface material [1].
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions and scoop size not given in the reviewed abstract. The full Scott and Roberson paper was not reviewed.

examples.name: Apollo Self-Recording Penetrometer (SRP)
examples.description: The Self-Recording Penetrometer was designed for astronaut use and was employed on Apollo 15 and Apollo 16 [6]. It measured penetration against force in the upper lunar soil. Strength parameters were derived with bearing-capacity theory, using wedge bearing-capacity factors modified for cone shape, and porosity was identified as the dominant controlling variable for a given soil [6]. The mass, cone diameter and overall dimensions of the SRP were not verified in the sources read for this article, so they are not stated here.
examples.qualification: Hardware mass and dimensions not verified. The statements above come from search-result text for the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report, because the full document could not be retrieved.

examples.name: Apollo 14 penetrometer, soil mechanics trench and transporter measurement programme
examples.description: The Apollo 14 soil-mechanics results were derived from a simple penetrometer, a special soil mechanics trench, the Modularized Equipment Transporter and core-tube samples [2]. Soil strength appeared higher near the Apollo 14 surface experiments package, and trench data suggested strength increases with depth. The abstract gives no numerical strength value, no friction angle and no numerical modulus [2]. The in-situ modulus, derived from seismic-wave velocity, is described as consistent with a terrestrial silty fine sand in lunar gravity, but no numerical value is given in the abstract [2]. The penetrometer mass and dimensions are not given [2].
examples.qualification: Penetrometer hardware details not given in the reviewed abstract. Full-text values were not reviewed.

examples.name: In-situ direct shear and sinkage device (Caltech, 2013)
examples.description: Jerves and colleagues describe a compact device for in-situ direct shear and sinkage tests on sand, clays and regolith, intended to be carried on a rover [4]. An inner open-bottomed box sits inside a larger open-bottomed box, and two rotating plates on the outer box swing outward so the inner box can shear without resistance from the surrounding soil. Outputs are Coulomb parameters (cohesion and internal friction angle) and Bekker parameters [4]. The experiments used a regolith simulant labelled `MMS<2mm` [4]. The size and mass of the device are not given, and the abstract does not state the test environment (vacuum or gravity). The device has not been flown, and mounting beneath a rover is described as a proposal only [4].
examples.qualification: Laboratory prototype record. Size, mass and test environment not given in the reviewed record. No flight heritage.

examples.name: NASA Regolith Utilization Multi-tool (RUM)
examples.description: NASA describes the RUM as a single robotic-arm end effector that collects regolith, sieves it, conveys it to an ISRU plant or other system, prepares sites and takes in-situ geotechnical measurements [5]. Its sieve sorts regolith below 1 mm at 10 to 40 g/s without clogging, and compaction can reach up to and beyond 100% relative density through tamping, vibration or both [5]. Shear is measured with an attached grader blade, pressure-sinkage tests characterise bearing and trafficability, and density is determined by photogrammetry and known-volume samples [5]. Components include two shaker motors and a vibro-compactor surface [5]. The page states that the technology is patent pending, does not state a technology readiness level, and gives no mass, dimensions or power [5].
examples.qualification: Patent-pending concept. No technology readiness level, demonstration or flight status stated in the reviewed page.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions are not publicly specified for the reviewed examples. The Surveyor sampler is described as an extendable scoop, and the Caltech device as a nested pair of open-bottomed boxes, but neither source gives sizes. Dimensions for a new system would have to follow from its test range, reaction loads and host mounting.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for any reviewed example. Mass drives launch, lander capacity, mounting design and robotic-arm load limits, so it must be fixed for a specific design before any integration assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for the reviewed examples. The RUM uses two shaker motors [5], so its vibration and compaction functions are likely to be significant power users, but the source does not quantify this.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The reviewed examples show several operating conditions. The Surveyor sampler's reported operating temperature range was +180 °F to −167 °F (approximately +82 °C to −111 °C) [1]. At Apollo 14, blowing dust reduced visibility less than on earlier missions, but eroded particles spread over a wide area around the touchdown point [2]. Dust and fine particles therefore need consideration for both sensing surfaces and moving mechanisms. The RUM sieve handles particles below 1 mm at 10 to 40 g/s [5]. Operations must also allow for soil variability, because the Apollo 14 study found shallow soil characteristics varied laterally and with depth [2]. The test environment of the Caltech device (vacuum or gravity) is not stated [4], and any flight test plan should document it.
article.limitations: In-situ results describe one test location and one depth profile, so they cannot characterise a region by themselves. Apollo 14 data varied across the site [2]. Historical strength values also depend on the theory and calibration used. The Apollo SRP analysis relies on bearing-capacity theory with assumed shape factors [6], and the Surveyor forces were inferred from motor current with preflight calibration [1]. Laboratory test beds use simulants, such as JSC-1a in the Agui study [3] and MMS<2mm in the Caltech study [4], which may not reproduce flight soil. The Caltech device has not been flown, and its test results are not reported in the sources read [4]. The RUM has no stated technology readiness level or demonstration [5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A material testing system could be delivered as a lander-mounted tool, as an astronaut-operated instrument, as a rover-mounted device or as a robotic-arm end effector. The reviewed sources cover lander-mounted and astronaut-operated tools, a rover-mounted proposal and a robotic-arm end effector. None of them asserts compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft. Orbiter and sample-return chains do not apply to this class of instrument, except that the RUM conveys collected regolith and could feed an ISRU plant [5].
transportation_process: Integrate the testing tool with its host: lander arm, rover mount or astronaut tool kit.
Launch the payload and transfer it towards the Moon.
Deliver it to the surface on a lander or rover.
Deploy it by robotic arm, rover mount or astronaut operation.
Position it on undisturbed regolith or within a prepared trench, then run the tests.
Store or transmit the recorded force, displacement and image data.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment depends on the design. The Surveyor sampler was operated from its lander [1]. The Apollo SRP was astronaut-operated [6]. The Apollo 14 soil-mechanics work used a penetrometer, a trench and the Modularized Equipment Transporter [2]. The RUM is a robotic-arm end effector [5], and the Caltech device is proposed for rover mounting [4].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Historical examples are the Surveyor 3 and Surveyor 7 sampler flights [1][3], the Apollo 14 soil-mechanics programme [2], and the Apollo 15 and Apollo 16 Self-Recording Penetrometer [6].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is assessed here. Mass, dimensions, mounting loads, power, data interface and thermal requirements are not stated for any example in the reviewed sources. Compatibility should be assessed once a specific design and host vehicle are defined.

article.historical_significance: The Surveyor and Apollo soil-mechanics experiments were early direct measurements of lunar surface mechanical behaviour [1][2][6]. Agui and colleagues revisited the Surveyor data with a laboratory replica and found that loose-bed bearing data compared well with the Surveyor flight data [3]. The Caltech device and the RUM show continued development of compact in-situ tools for rovers and ISRU [4][5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The name in-situ material testing system describes a class of tools rather than one design, so the examples should not be treated as interchangeable. The flown examples are historical, and their mass, dimensions and power are not verified here. The Apollo SRP statements rely on search-result text for the Apollo 16 Preliminary Science Report because the full document could not be retrieved [6]. The Agui abstract gives no bearing or excavation force values [3]. The Caltech abstract reports no test results [4]. The RUM has no stated technology readiness level and no demonstration status [5]. The NTRS scanned report for the Apollo soil-mechanics experiment could not be read as text. No image assets have been verified. The lunar location recommendation is deferred by the user and is not included.
